Letters to the Editor Related to New Topics
Qigong for Movement Disorders:
A Systematic Review
Parkinson’s disease (PD) or other types of movement disorders
occur worldwide in all ethnic groups and socioeconomic
classes.1,2 Because of the chronic and debilitating symptoms of
PD or other types of movement disorders patients often use
complementary medicine. 3–5 One such treatment option is
qigong. Qigong is a form of traditional Asian medicine, which
incorporates exercise for posture, coordination of different
breathing patterns, movement, and meditation. It has been
reported that qigong has beneﬁcial effects in improving psycho-
logical health, reducing high blood pressure and pain, and mod-
ulating neurohormone and immune systems.
6–9 It, therefore,
seems pertinent to evaluate the effectiveness of qigong for
movement disorders. The objective of this systematic review is
to summarize and critically assess the evidence of qigong for
treating movement disorders.
Databases systematically searched from their respective
inceptions through to March 2008 were: Medline, AMED,
British Nursing Index, CINAHL, EMBASE, PsycInfo, Sco-
pus, The Cochrane Library 2008 (Issue 1), 6 Korean Medical
Databases (Korean Studies Information, DBPIA, Korea Insti-
tute of Science and Technology Information, Research Infor-
mation Center for Health Database, KoreanMed, and National
Assembly Library), 4 Chinese Medical Databases (China
Academic Journal, Century Journal Project, China Doctor/
Master Dissertation Full Text DB, and China Proceedings
Conference Full Text DB), the Qigong and Energy Medicine
Database (Version 7.4, Qigong Institute, Melon Park, CA),
and Electronic Japan Science and Technology Information
Aggregator. The search phrase used was ‘ ‘qigong AND (cor-
ticobasal degeneration OR dyskinesias (paroxysmal) OR dys-
tonia OR essential tremor OR hereditary spastic paraplegia
OR Huntington’s disease OR multiple system atrophy OR
myoclonus OR Parkinson’s disease OR progressive supranu-
clear palsy OR restless legs syndrome OR Rett syndrome OR
spasticity OR Sydenham’s Chorea OR tardive dyskinesia OR
Tourette’s syndrome OR Wilson disease).’ ’ The references in
all located articles were manually searched for further rele-
vant articles. All prospective clinical studies related to the
effects of qigong on movement disorders were included. No
language restrictions were imposed. Dissertations and
abstracts were included. Hard copies of all articles were
obtained and read in full. A modiﬁed Jadad score
10 was used
whereby a point was given for blinding if the outcome asses-
sor was blinded.
One hundred and forty-seven articles were located (Sup-
plement Table 1 shows the reason for exclusion), of which
four
11–14 were included (see Fig. 1). Of the four included
studies (Table 1), one randomized clinical trial (RCT) 11
failed to show qigong to be superior to aerobic exercise in
terms of the Uniﬁed PD Rating Scale (UPDRS), depression
and PD Questionnaires-39 (PDQ-39). Another RCT
12 found
no effects of qigong on locomotor ability when compared
with tai chi. This study was published only as a proceeding,
and hence it had not been formally peer reviewed (it also
lacked essential details). Furthermore, these two RCT com-
pared qigong to aerobic exercise
11 or tai chi 12 without dem-
onstrating the effectiveness of the treatment. 11,12 Whether the
ﬁndings of no difference compared with aerobic exercise or
tai chi reﬂects equivalence of effect or ineffectiveness is as

yet unclear. The third RCT
13 reported effects of qigong
adjunct to usual care on the UPDRS III but failed to do on
the PDQ when compared with usual care control. However,
an add-on treatment provides little information about any
speciﬁc effect s. The remaining study
14 was a nonrandomized
clinical trial, which showed superior effects of qigong on se-
verity of PD compared with no treatment. This type of study

was open to selection bias that can lead to false-positive
results. None of trials employed assessor blinding and con-
tained detection bias.
One trial originated from Germany, and one trial was con-
ducted in Italy, one trial was from USA, and one trial was from
China. It seems therefore likely that the effects are not crucially
depending on any cultural context. However, more research would
be required to address this interesting point systematically.
Perhaps, the most important ﬁnding of this systematic
review is that there have been very few rigorous trials of the
effects of qigong on movement disorders. All of the included
trials assessed effects of qigong for PD. The evidence is
insufﬁcient to suggest qigong is an effective modality for
treating movement disorders, speciﬁcally PD. Further
research is required to investigate whether there are speciﬁc
beneﬁts of qigong for such patients.

Cerebellar and Pyramidal Dysfunctions,
Palpebral Ptosis and Weakness As Presenting
Symptoms of PARK-2
Video
Parkin gene mutations are a common cause of early-onset par-
kinsonism with autosomal recessive inheritance (PARK-2).
We report the case of a patient with an ataxic-spastic
syndrome at the age of 3 years, and typical parkinsonism
several years later associa ted with palpebral ptosis and
muscle weakness.
The patient is a 30-year-old man. He was adopted at the
age of 2 years; hence no information is available about fam-
ily history, birth circumstances, and developmental mile-
stones. Symptoms, namely unst eady gait, bilateral palpebral
ptosis, and weakness, ﬁrst appeared when he was 3 years
old. At age 7, he was affected by bradykinesia, lower limb
dystonia, and rigidity. At age 15, his neurological examina-
tion showed ataxic-spastic gait, symmetrical parkinsonism,
dystonia, which was more severe at the lower limbs, palpe-
bral ptosis, and muscle weakness. A mild increase of serum
lactate (2.1 mmoles/L; n.v. 03–1.5 mmoles/L) suggested a
defect in mitochondrial energy metabolism. A quadriceps
muscle biopsy was performed, and histology showed no
signiﬁcant alteration; ultrastr uctural examination revealed a
drastic reduction in subsarcolemmal and intermyoﬁbrillar
mitochondria and a widespread increase of glycogen

sponsive to L-dopa and muscle weakness. Cerebellar dys-
function has been described in a few patients with parkin
gene mutations.
1–3 In all previously described patients, cer-
ebellar dysfunction developed in concomitance with or
some years after extrapyramidal signs, whereas our patient
had ataxic-spastic gait as part of the early onset symptoma-
tology. Parkin mRNA is highl y expressed in the cerebel-
lum,
4 supporting the data that parkin gene dysfunction may
be associated with cerebellar impairment in few cases. The
mutations detected in our patient are located in critical
regions of parkin:
5 the large deletion of three exons
includes exon 2, whic h contains the ubiquitin-like domain,
whereas the C820T mutation is in the RING ﬁnger-like
motif that is crucial for the m aintenance of normal parkin
protein function. 6 The association of these two mutations
might explain the very early on set and the atypical features
in our patient.
In this patient, the dopamine transporter loss was symmet-
rical and severe, the dopamine D 2 receptors in the striatum
were decreased, both ﬁndings have been already reported in
parkin-related parkinsonism.7,8
In addition, our patient showed atypical MRI ﬁndings.
Corticospinal tract involvement at MRI has been reported
only in a few patients with parkin gene mutations and atypi-
cal clinical features. 3
Moreover, our patient muscle biopsy demonstrated a
severe decrease of subsarcolemmal and intermyoﬁbrillar
mitochondria and an increase of glycogen. To date, no mor-
phological alterations of muscle have been reported in par-
kin-related parkinsonism. However, parkin is known to exert
an antiapoptotic effect and a neuroprotective function that is
abrogated by disease-related mutations. 9
Greene et al. 10 have created a Drosophila parkin-null mu-
tant showing reduced lifespan, locomotor defects, and male
sterility. The locomotor abnormalities have been related to
increased apoptotic muscle cells and evidence of early mito-
chondrial changes.
This report further expands t he spectrum of the clinical
manifestations of parkin-related parkinsonism and high-
lights a possible occurrence o f muscle alterations in ab-
sence of mitochondrial DNA mutations. Although unlikely
due to the rarity of parkin mutations, we cannot exclude
that the patient carries additional mutations in other genes
or modiﬁers.

Nucleus Ventralis Oralis Deep Brain
Stimulation in Postanoxic Dystonia
Video
Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the thalamus, zona incerta,
subthalamic nucleus, and pallidum has been used for the
treatment of dystonia.
1 Reports on thalamic DBS for dystonia
were published as early as 1977. 2,3 Thalamic stimulation may
increase the dystonic symptoms, especially when the Vim nu-
cleus is the target of the stimulation.
4
However, targeting the thalamus was abandoned because
several publications suggested that the globus pallidus
internus (GPi) is a better choice for stereotaxy in patients
with dystonia.
5–9 An interesting issue is what happens in
case of a structural lesion in the GPi? Structural lesions of
the GPi are not considered an ab solute contraindication for
the DBS electrode placement; however, thalamic nuclei

female hemidystonic patient with bilateral structural abnor-
malities of the GPi, due to pos tanoxic damage, who was
treated successfully with DBS of ventralis oralis anterior
(Voa) nucleus.
A 37-year-old woman presented with a right side hemidys-
tonia. There was no family history of dystonic conditions.
The pregnancy was normal and the delivery was spontaneous
at term, but complicated by prolonged labor and insufﬁcient
blood supply from the umbilical artery. The perinatal adapta-
tion and motor development were normal.
At the age of 3, she started to develop a right lower limb
dystonia that led to walking impairment. Hemidystonia devel-
oped progressively, and within years walking became impos-
sible. The patient was wheelchair bound and required assis-
tance in dressing and hygiene, for the last 9 years (Video 1).
The neurological examination revealed a dystonic posture
of the right side of her body, with the lower limb more
severely affected. The right hand was kept periodically in a
hyper ﬂexed claw-like fashion, and the foot exhibited perma-
nent dorsiﬂexion and extortion. She had normal power of all
muscle groups on the affected right side. The tendon reﬂexes
were symmetrical, and no pathological reﬂexes were present.
The neurological examination of the left side of the body
was normal. Her vital signs and general physical examination
were unremarkable.
The laboratory tests, including cooper level and cerulo-
plasmin, were within normal limits. Preoperative magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) showed bilateral postanoxic lesions
in the globus pallidus (Fig. 1). The GPi was totally damaged
bilaterally. Several medications (
L-dopa, tizarnidine, baclofen,
tetrabenazine) had been unsuccessful in improving the
patient’s symptoms.
Dystonia was videotaped and assessed using the Burke,
Fahn, Marsden Dystonia rating scale (BFMDRS) preopera-
tively and postoperatively at monthly intervals for the ﬁrst
year and at 3-month intervals thereafter.
The patient underwent a stereotactic implantation of an
electrode (model 3387, Medtronic, Minneapolis, MN) in the
left nucleus Voa. The correct position of the electrode was
evaluated postoperatively by MRI scan and the Frame-Link
software. The ﬁnal electrode position was at the base of the
Voa nucleus close to the Voa/Vop border. The active con-
tacts of the electrode were the contacts 0 and 1 inside the
Voa nucleus (Fig. 2). The initial postoperative stimulation
parameters were 2.5 volts, 185 Hz, 250 lsec, with monopo-
lar stimulation on contacts 0 and 1, respectively. Further

adjustments of the stimulation parameters were performed
during the follow-up period. The amplitude ranged between
2.5 and 3.6 volts, pulse width ranged between 250 and
450 lsec while the frequency was kept stable at 185 Hz.
The functional status and the daily life activities were grad-
ually improved after 6 months postoperatively, having the
best results on the 12 month follow-up assessment. The
good outcome lasts up today (28 months postoperatively).
The BFM dystonia scale improved by 76% in total (dis-
ability scale improved from 13/30 to 6/30 and movement
scale improved from 20/120 to 2/120). The patient is now
able to walk again after 9 years use of a wheelchair with
the stimulator always on function (Video 2). She still suf-
fers intermittently, under stress conditions, from minor jerky
movements of the right hand, but the movements of the
right upper limb are less prominent compared with the pre-
operative condition.

Structural brain lesions are common in secondary dysto-
nia.10 It is possible that lesions of the GPi may result in loss of
inhibitory pallidal projections to the thalamus and thus, pro-
voke the hyperkinetic condition. The main stimuli of the pal-
lidum are via the Voa and the centromedian-parafascicular nu-
cleus. Targeting the Voa nucleus for DBS could act directly on
the last distal link in the retroactive feedback system to the
motor cortex of the GPi. To our knowledge, this is the only
case with follow-up up to 28 months. A similar report, with
only a 4-month follow-up, has been published by Ghika
et al.
11 A patient with generalized postanoxic dystonia was
treated initially with DBS of GPi and then with DBS of Voa.
The patient showed a dramatic improvement after the Voa
DBS procedure. The placement of the electrode in the Voa nu-
cleus was conﬁrmed by autopsy. In our case, the correct posi-
tion of the electrodes in the Voa nucleus was conﬁrmed by a
postoperative MRI, the Frame-Link software and was further
validated by image registration and fusion software.
12
Our report concurs with that of Ghika, that the Voa nu-
cleus may well be an effective alternative when there is a
damaged GPi or in cases of GPi DBS failure. In addition to
the report of Ghika, the follow-up of our patient, over a pe-
riod of 28 months, revealed that the Voa nucleus offers, not
only temporary, but satisfactory long-term results.
Nevertheless, since our case reﬂects just the experience
on one patient, further studies are deemed necessary to
achieve a more informed perceptive as to who would bene-
ﬁt from thalamic or GPi DBS.

Neurodegenerative Parkinsonism and
Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia
with a Twinkle Mutation
Video
A prominent role for mitochondrial dysfunction in the patho-
genesis of Parkinson’s disease (PD) has been suspected ever
since the description of parkinsonism caused by the com-
plex I inhibitor 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine
(MPTP).
1 The connection with mitochondrial dysfunction
was further strengthened by linkage of recessive PD to muta-
tions in PINK1, a gene encoding a mitochondrial kinase. 1 In
addition, mutations in POLG, the gene encoding polymerase
g, the only mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) polymerase, can
cause parkinsonism, usually in combination with progressive
external opthalmoplegia (PEO). 2 We report a patient with
neurodegenerative parkinsonism, PEO, and a mutation in
PEO1, the gene for the mtDNA helicase Twinkle, a protein
that closely collaborates with polymerase g in the replication
and maintenance of mtDNA.
3
The proband (subject III-1), a 51-year-old Flemish right-
handed professional cook, presented in 2007 with a 1-year
history of slowly progressive rest tremor of the right hand
and, to a lesser extent, the right leg. Emotional stress tended
to aggravate the tremor. His handwriting had become smaller
and he reported slight difﬁculty buttoning clothes with the
right hand. He had experienced reduced sense of smell since
many years. Interestingly, he had noticed slowly progressive
eyelid drooping without diplopia since the age of 30 years.
He had undergone corrective eyelid surgery twice (around
1997 and 2002), with only temporary improvement. His med-
ical history was otherwise unremarkable and he took no
medication.
The patient had no children or siblings. According to the
patient, his mother (subject II-1), maternal aunt (subject II-2),
and grandmother (subject I-1) had droopy eyelids, but no
tremor or Parkinsonism (Fig. 1A).
Clinical examination of III-1 in 2007 (see video) revealed
moderate bilateral ptosis and severe restriction of eye move-
ments in all gaze directions. The ptosis and ophthalmoparesis
were not fatigable. There was mild hypokinesia, intermittent
rest tremor, and cogwheel rigidity of the right arm. Gait was
normal except for reduced right arm swing. Cognition,
speech, muscle strength, tendon reﬂexes, plantar reﬂexes,
coordination, and sensation were normal. There was no mus-
cle atrophy.
123I-FP-CIT SPECT imaging of the dopamine transporter
in 2007 revealed substantially reduced putaminal binding on
both sides (Fig. 1B). Brain MRI in 2008 was normal. Needle
electromyography of the anterior tibial, deltoid, iliopsoas, and
orbicular oris muscles and nerve conduction studies in 2007
were normal. A deltoid muscle biopsy was performed in
1997; light microscopy including hematoxylin/eosin, Gomori
trichrome, succinate dehydrogenase, and cytochrome c oxi-
dase staining was normal. Sequencing of the exons of the
POLG gene was normal. Sequencing of the PEO1 gene
showed a heterozygous mutation predicting a R334Q substi-
tution in Twinkle.
Dopaminergic medication was proposed, but the patient
preferred to wait because functional impairment was only
mild.
We provide the ﬁrst description of a patient with PEO,

parkinsonism, a Twinkle R334Q substitution and a normal
POLG sequence. PEO1 mutations are an established cause of
autosomal dominant PEO.
4 It appears highly likely that this
patient’s parkinsonism was also caused by the PEO1 muta-
tion, for two reasons. First, a similar clinical syndrome of
PEO with subsequent development of parkinsonism has been
clearly associated with POLG mutations.
2 Given the intricate
functional interplay between polymerase g and Twinkle in
the maintenance of mtDNA, 3 extensive phenotypic overlap
between PEO1 and POLG mutations would be biologically
plausible. Second, Baloh et al. recently reported a family

The R334Q substitution occurs in a highly conserved resi-

in 2 patients. One had a heterozygous R334Q mutation and

6 The second patient had a heterozygous
R334Q mutation associated with sporadic PEO and parkin-

it more difﬁcult to establish the contribution of the Twinkle

Dopamine transporter imaging, which had not previously
been performed in patients with parkinsonism and PEO1
mutations, was clearly abnormal in our proband and indicated
the neurodegenerative nature of his parkinsonism.
In conclusion, one should consider the possibility of muta-
tions in PEO1 and not just POLG when confronted with the
co-occurrence of PEO and parkinsonism. In addition, this
case further supports a role for mitochondrial dysfunction in
PD pathogenesis.

Although tremor is the most frequent extrapyramidal mani-
festation in MS, parkinsonism, dystonia, choreoathetosis, bal-
lism, and myoclonus have been reported. 1 The majority of
MS cases with movement disorders have no evident ana-
tomic/phenotypic correlates with brain magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) studies 1 This suggests that these manifesta-
tions are secondary to immune and neurodegenerative com-
ponents. We discuss the case of a woman who presented
with evidence of MS and dystonia with subsequent evolution
of parkinsonism.
Three months postpartum, a 38-year-old previously healthy
woman suffered balance and gait difﬁculties followed by the
onset of paroxysmal dystonia of the right leg. Urinary fre-
quency, urgency, and incontinence began 1 year earlier. She
subsequently experienced progressive dysarthria, lower limb
weakness, and decreased visual acuity of left eye. Examina-
tion at that point revealed masked facies and mild lower ex-
tremity weakness (spastic paraparesis, R >L). Tandem gait
was abnormal.
Over the following year, she progressed with generalized
slowing of movement, postural instability, loss of dexterity
and coordination, persistent bilateral limb and cervical dysto-
nia. She became dependent for bathing and toileting. Reex-
amination revealed a labile affect but intact cognition. She
had cervical dystonia with generalized rigidity and marked
bradykinesia (R > L). Mild left upper limb dysmetria was
present, arm swing was reduced, and her gait was slow. Ret-
ropulsion was also detected. Generalized hyperreﬂexia and a
right Babinski sign were observed.
Over the subsequent year, she developed mild cognitive
impairment, facial myokymia, right nasolabial ﬂattening,
increased tremor, and postural instability. Highlights of her
examination are presented in Video 1. Additional examina-
tions showed progressive deterioration including a Romberg
sign, clonus at the knees with bilateral Babinski signs. The
progression of the disease as measured using the Uniﬁed Par-
kinson’s disease rating scale (UPDRS)
2 and the expanded
disability status scale (EDSS) 3 is presented in Table 1.
Serial brain MRIs over 2 years showed an increasing white
matter lesion load and progressive diffuse atrophy (Fig. 1).
Notably, there were no enhancing lesions or any lesions
involving basal ganglia or midbrain. An elevated IgG index
and oligoclonal bands were found in the cerebrospinal ﬂuid,
and visual evoked potentials revealed prolonged P-100 wave
latency in the left eye. A diagnosis of primary progressive
multiple sclerosis (PPMS) was established, employing the re-
vised McDonald criteria,
4 with parkinsonism secondary to
MS. Extensive laboratory investigations (including genetic
testing) excluded other neurological disease. However, anti-
basal ganglionic antibodies (ABGA) were detected by west-
ern immunoblotting and neuron-speciﬁc (gamma) enolase,
and pyruvate kinase M1 were reported positive.
5 Her [18F]-2-
ﬂuoro-deoxy-D-glucose PET brain scan was normal.
Treatment with glatiramer acetate, carbidopa/ L-dopa, and
amantadine did not alter her progressive course. She did not
respond to a 5-day course of intravenous methylprednisolone
or to IVIG. There was a mild long-term beneﬁt in bradykine-
sia from amantadine.

a spectrum of clinical phenomena that include steadily wor-
sening symptoms and signs over ‡6 months. These phenom-

warranted because presence of such antibody may be the sub-

Stiff-Person syndrome (SPS), is a rare and disabling disor-
der characterized by rigidity and painful episodic spasms that

involve axial and limb musculature with continuous, involun-
tary motor-unit activity (CMUA) at rest in electrophysiologi-
cal studies.
1 SPS can be subdivided into stiff-trunk syndrome,
stiff-limb syndrome (SLS), and progressive encephalomyelitis
with rigidity. 1 The cause of this disorder is unknown; how-
ever, an autoimmune pathogenesis is suspected. 1
We report a patient diagnosed with stiff-three limbs syn-
drome (STLS), without CMUA, successfully treated with in-
travenous immunoglobulin.
An 11-year-old girl was admitted to the Movement Disor-
ders Unit of the Hospital de Clı ´nicas of the Federal Univer-
sity of Parana´ (Brazil) with a 2-year history of limb ‘ ‘paraly-
sis’ ’ and dysarthria. Symptoms started 1 week after an upper
respiratory tract viral infection in the form of progressive,
ﬂuctuating, and painful rigidity in the right upper and both
lower limbs. Initially she complained of frequent falls and
later rigidity in the affected limbs became ﬁxed, with dis-
abling gait disturbance and associated with severe dysarthria
(video 1). Previous personal and family medical histories
were unremarkable.
Neurological examination showed severe dysarthria with
no other abnormalities in cranial nerves assessment. Lower
limbs and right upper limbs showed diffuse livedo reticularis
with skin coldness in comparison with the nonaffected left
upper limb. Limbs were normotrophic with moderate to
severe rigidity in the lower limbs and right upper limb, with
proportionate proximal and distal distribution. The left upper

Extrapyramidal Reaction to Ondansetron
and Propofol
Video
Ondansetron is a 5-HT 3 receptor antagonist, which at the
time of its introduction was not expected to cause extrapyra-
midal side effects. Over the past decade isolated cases of
ondansetron related extrapyramidal side effects have been
reported.
1–4 Propofol has also been reported to cause a wide
range of involuntary movements including seizures. 5
We report a patient with a dramatic onset of unusual and
complex involuntary movements during recovery from anes-
thesia. Propofol had been used for induction and ondansetron
for prophylaxis against postoperative nausea. The nature of
the involuntary movements associated with these agents is
discussed and a video documentation of the movements seen
in the reported patient is provided.
A 26-year-old man underwent a tonsillectomy under gen-
eral anesthesia with propofol and desﬂurane. Immediately af-
ter the surgery he received 5 cc of 0.25% bupivacaine into
each tonsillar fossa as prophylaxis for postoperative pain.
Four milligram of intravenous ondansetron was given as pro-

administration of ondansetron he developed involuntary
movements involving his limbs and trunk. These included
action tremors, dystonic trunk movements, with frequent ﬂex-

movements were random and unaccompanied by tonic or
clonic activity. They seemed to be exacerbated with voli-
tional activation, and were relieved to some extent with rest.
Holding the limb down suppressed some of the movements.
Frequently a predisposition towards jerky arching of the back
was noted, suggestive of ‘ ‘partial opisthotonus.’ ’ His speech
output was interrupted by short bouts of what was felt to be
diaphragmatic contractions and possibly pharyngeal and
laryngeal spasms. Despite these involuntary movements he
could perform goal directed movements with his limbs. His
orientation and ability to respond to questions was unaf-
fected. Upper and lower limb tone was normal. No weakness
was identiﬁed and there was no clouding of sensorium. These
movements subsided in 2 hours. He received 25 mg of intra-
venous diphenhydramine, 2 mg of intravenous midazolam,
and 2 mg of intravenous lorazepam. None of these interven-
tions appeared to suppress the involuntary movements. He
past history was remarkable for occasional seizures as a
child. He was on no medications. His family history was
unremarkable. He was discharged the following day and at
follow-up 3 months after the episode reported no symptoms.
In our patient the nature of the involuntary movements
was very similar to the involuntary movements that have
been described with ondansetron. The temporal relationship
of the onset of the involuntary movements following admin-
istration of ondansetron makes it the most likely responsible
agent. It is possible that the involuntary movements were
related at least in part to propofol. Either has been suspect in
other reported cases also.
6 The differential diagnosis of invol-
untary movements following emergence from anesthesia can
also include postanesthetic shivering characterized by diffuse
involvement and rigidity, local anesthetic reaction, and emer-
gence delirium. The nature of the involuntary movements
associated with ondansetron or propofol has not been well
characterized and no video documentation exists. Most of the
available information is in the anesthesiology literature.
The presentation of involuntary movements related to
ondansetron use is often dramatic and has been variably char-
acterized as chorea, dystonia, seizure-like activity, ‘ ‘stimulus-
sensitive generalized clonus’ ’ or simply as jerky movements
that may resemble seizures.
1–4 As in our patient, attenuation
of the movements by holding the limbs has been reported. 4
At times the movements have been initially considered to be
related to anxiety or be psychogenic in nature. 4,6 The extrap-
yramidal side effects of ondansetron may be dose related. 1 A
prior history of drug-induced extrapyramidal side effects may
be a predisposing factor.
4 Animal studies have shown that
ondansetron reduces increased mesolimbic dopamine activity
and antagonizes increased locomotor activity caused by mes-
olimbic dopamine excess. 7 Oral ondansetron has been used
to treat levodopa-associated psychosis. 7
Propofol administration has been associated with involun-
tary movements that have been variable characterized as
dystonia, chorea, myoclonus, tremulousness, opisthotonus,

seizures, ‘ ‘neuroexcitatory movements,’ ’ ‘ ‘seizure-like phe-
nomenon,’ ’ ‘ ‘increased tone with twitching and rhythmic
movements not perceived as generalized tonic clonic
seizures.’ ’
5 The involuntary movements seen with propofol
use are more commonly seen during induction or emergence
rather than maintenance.
5 It has been speculated that these
movements may result from disparate gamma-aminobutyric
acid receptor modulation by propofol.
Ondansetron can rarely induce extrapyramidal reactions in
susceptible individuals. Similar involuntary movements can
also occur with propofol use and these considerations should
be included in the differential diagnosis of involuntary move-
ments seen during recovery from anesthesia. The involuntary
movements have a dramatic presentation and excellent prog-
nosis. They should be differentiated from seizures. Individual
susceptibility may be related to genetic factors, dose, prior
history of seizures or extrapyramidal reactions.

Stiff-Three Limbs Syndrome
Video
Stiff-Person syndrome (SPS), is a rare and disabling disor-
der characterized by rigidity and painful episodic spasms that

segments.text:
involve axial and limb musculature with continuous, involun-
tary motor-unit activity (CMUA) at rest in electrophysiologi-
cal studies.
1 SPS can be subdivided into stiff-trunk syndrome,
stiff-limb syndrome (SLS), and progressive encephalomyelitis
with rigidity. 1 The cause of this disorder is unknown; how-
ever, an autoimmune pathogenesis is suspected. 1
We report a patient diagnosed with stiff-three limbs syn-
drome (STLS), without CMUA, successfully treated with in-
travenous immunoglobulin.
An 11-year-old girl was admitted to the Movement Disor-
ders Unit of the Hospital de Clı ´nicas of the Federal Univer-
sity of Parana´ (Brazil) with a 2-year history of limb ‘ ‘paraly-
sis’ ’ and dysarthria. Symptoms started 1 week after an upper
respiratory tract viral infection in the form of progressive,
ﬂuctuating, and painful rigidity in the right upper and both
lower limbs. Initially she complained of frequent falls and
later rigidity in the affected limbs became ﬁxed, with dis-
abling gait disturbance and associated with severe dysarthria
(video 1). Previous personal and family medical histories
were unremarkable.
Neurological examination showed severe dysarthria with
no other abnormalities in cranial nerves assessment. Lower
limbs and right upper limbs showed diffuse livedo reticularis
with skin coldness in comparison with the nonaffected left
upper limb. Limbs were normotrophic with moderate to
severe rigidity in the lower limbs and right upper limb, with
proportionate proximal and distal distribution. The left upper

segments.text:
limb showed no signs of abnormal tone strength, despite the
subjective complaint of paralysis. Deep tendon reﬂexes were
brisk, symmetric, and plantar reﬂexes were ﬂexor. Laboratory
tests included normal leukocytes, red cells, and platelet
counts; normal plasma glucose, creatinine, electrolytes, anti-
cardiolipin, antinuclear antibodies, TSH and CK levels; nor-
mal erythrocyte sedimentation rate; negative syphilis, hepati-
tis B/C, and HIV serologies; cerebral spinal ﬂuid analysis
was unremarkable as well as brain and spinal chord MRI and
electromyography with nerve conduction studies of the upper
and lower limbs and paraspinal muscles. Plasma autoantibod-
ies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD) were positive
(2.6 U/mL).
The symptoms remained unchanged during treatment with
baclofen (up to 40 mg/day, for 1 month) or diazepam (30
mg/day for 20 days). After 3 months, intravenous immuno-
globulin was started and repeated for 1 year (initial dose:
0.4 g/kg/day for ﬁve consecutive days, followed by monthly
doses of 0.4 g/kg administered for 1 day). During this pe-
riod, the patient showed signiﬁcant improvement of rigidity
and gait performance with mild improvement in dysarthria
(video 2: after 1 year of follow-up and video 3: after 3
years of follow-up).
The case reported here describ es a patient with a distinct
clinical presentation of SPS, namely painful stiffness in
three limbs and dysarthria, with no features such as sphinc-
ter disturbances, truncal rigid ity, exaggerated lumbar lordo-
sis, or CMUA.
